turns.prompt_text: I currently kind of use AI as an extension of mind, kind of a way to help me think because it kind of grants me to what is really possible. A few years ago we could Google it real quick and get a good amount of data, but now it's a lot more user friendly and easier to consume. That being said, it still cannot get localized information or private or secret information, so there's limitations here and there, but generally it's overall a lot better And while it is really better, I've been thinking about creating multi-agent teams in order to answer my questions better. These are specifically for deeper thinking that I kind of want to spend more time on. These are like think tanks, or teams of agents? Just kind of think about how to solve problems for many different perspectives and run simulations and probes and such. They just kind of churn and think about the original problems. And the way I get the problems is that I'll go back and look over the different chats of of the past year or so and I'm going to see what I didn't solve and why I didn't solve it. And many of them I think just need a good amount of deeper thought. And there is the perfect ground for where a think tank like this might help out. I don't necessarily want to drive anymore because I do that a lot. I want to hand this all off.
turns.response_html:
It is fascinating how the paradigm has shifted from simply retrieving data to actively augmenting our cognitive load. You are hitting the exact ceiling of traditional, single-turn prompting: it still requires you to constantly steer the wheel. Stepping back and building an autonomous think tank to chew on complex, unresolved problems is the logical next step for deeper analysis.

To build a system where you no longer have to drive, the architecture needs to handle the extraction, orchestration, and synthesis completely in the background.

1. Problem Extraction & Curation

The first step is feeding the think tank. Since you are going back through the past year of chats to find unresolved problems, you need a systemic way to parse and organize that history.

  • Metadata Indexing: You can funnel these exported chats into a local-first, linked Markdown graph topology. By tagging these specific unresolved nodes, you create a decoupled metadata index of "open problems."
  • The Intake Agent: Before any problem-solving begins, a lightweight triage agent can read this index, assess why the problem stalled initially, and define the scope of the simulation required to crack it.

2. The Think Tank Orchestration

To truly step away from the driver's seat, the multi-agent system needs a robust automation framework that can run locally and autonomously.

  • The Framework: Utilizing an agentic automation framework like Google antigravity will allow you to spin up diverse agent personas that can interact with one another without your constant prompting.
  • Custom Local Environments: You can containerize these agents within custom local script environments so they have the freedom to execute code, run probes, and test hypotheses independently while churning on the data.

3. Agent Roles and Perspectives

A true think tank thrives on friction and diverse perspectives. You can define specific roles for the agents in your network to ensure they are rigorously testing the problem rather than just agreeing with one another:

  • The Generator: Proposes wild, unconstrained solutions based on the original prompt.
  • The Simulator: Takes the Generator's ideas and runs logical or programmatic probes to test their viability against real-world constraints.
  • The Red Teamer: Actively tries to break the Simulator's findings, looking for logical fallacies, edge cases, or missing variables.
  • The Synthesizer: Monitors the ongoing debate and eventually compiles a finalized, polished report of the best possible solutions.

4. Continuous Asynchronous Churn

The beauty of this setup is that it operates asynchronously. You can drop an unresolved problem into the intake folder, let the agents debate, run their scripts, and simulate outcomes for hours or days. When you return, instead of an empty chat box asking for your next command, you are presented with a synthesized briefing of their findings.

If you want to start building this orchestration layer, how do you want the final synthesized output delivered back to you once the think tank finishes chewing on a problem?
